l: Nemean victory of Pytheas, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a pankration victory [won at Nemea while Pytheas was a boy] Pytheas's Nemean victory brought honor to the Aiakidai and to Aigina. Nemea is described as favorable to him.

l: Phylakidas of Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Phylakidas of Aigina is Lampon’s youngest son and Pytheas’s brother, an athlete and pankration winner. He wins at the Isthmian Games, gaining double glory there and a pankratiast’s crown at Nemea. His victories prompt praise in Isthmian Odes IV and V and celebrate his family’s athletic achievements.

l: Lampon, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Lampon, son of Kleonikos and father of successful athlete sons including Phylakidas, is praised for disciplined practice. He honors Hesiod, urges his sons to practice, kindly welcomes strangers, seeks the just mean, and speaks in accord with his thoughts, sharpening athletes like a Naxian whetstone.

l: sweet song, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: A sweet song travels from Aigina on ships and boats, spreading news of Pytheas's victory rather than standing idle.

l: Aiakidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Aiakidai are a lineage of warrior heroes, sons of Endais, sprung from Kronos, Zeus, and golden nymphs. They honor and pray for Aigina beside Zeus Hellenios’s altar. Their family includes Phokos, and after a portentous unjust deed they are expelled from Oinone. Athletic victories, including Praxidamas’s Olympic wreath, and Achilles’s slaying of Memnon spread their glory widely.

l: Phokos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Phokos, goddess-born son of Aiakos and Psamatheia, embodies royal strength until Endais’s sons kill him and leave the island.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Aigina is a beloved island and city, praised as a commonwealth of equal laws and a place of long-honored valour. Through union with Zeus she is mother of Aiakos, and his sons form her heroic lineage and subjects for song. Her seamen helped deliver Salamis. The records move from her divine and familial association to civic praise, martial service, and poetic honor.

l: Euthymenes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Euthymenes, maternal uncle and kinsman of Pytheas and Phylakidas, wins at Aigina and honors Pytheas by following his footsteps.

l: victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_honoured_by song [in games] Victory is celebrated as the result of successful effort in games and as a source of honor. Phylakidas’s pankration victory is marked with a crown, a fleecy fillet, and a new hymn.

l: Alkimidas, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Alkimidas is a boys’ wrestling winner at Nemea, trained by Melesias and belonging to the Bassid clan. Descended from Praxidamas, he returns victorious from Nemea; his win is his house’s five-and-twentieth athletic honour and evidence of excellence across generations, though Olympic wreaths were denied by lot.

l: Praxidamas, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Praxidamas, an Aiakidai athlete descended from Sokleides, won at Olympia, five times at Isthmos, and three at Nemea; he honored Sokleides and preceded his son Alkimidas.

l: Bassid clan, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The Bassid clan, an old renowned lineage associated with Aigina, gains poetic fame from ancestral noble acts as Nemean Ode VI honors its house and athletic achievements.

l: boys' wrestling-match, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a athletic contest [won by Alkimidas] The boys' wrestling-match is won by Alkimidas. His success is described as following the ordinance of Zeus and as proving him a successful hunter in his wrestling quest.

l: the ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: honours Alkimidas [for his wrestling victory] The ode honors Alkimidas's victory and praises the athletic achievements of his family and the Bassid clan. It recalls victories at Olympia, Isthmos, Nemea, and Pytho, and closes by praising Melesias's training of Alkimidas.

l: hereditary athletic excellence, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a family disposition [appearing in alternate generations] Hereditary athletic excellence is illustrated by the comparison of Alkimidas's family with fruitful fields that yield and then gather strength. Alkimidas follows the athletic path of Praxidamas, while the family record includes distinguished athletes in alternating generations.

l: Sogenes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Sogenes, son of Thearion from Aigina, wins the boys' pentathlon and gains distinction. Celebrated by Pindar as a victor who lives beside Herakles' sacred places with devotion, he is prayed for lasting strength, prosperity, and honor with his family.

l: Thearion, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Thearion, father of Sogenes, gains a fair measure of bliss through daring and sound understanding; praised as Pindar’s friend, he is wished enduring prosperity with his descendants.

l: Odysseus, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Odysseus is a famed figure whose poetic renown exceeds his toils, as persuasive songs make even deceptive stories believed. He secretly wins the Danaoi’s vote for golden arms, a contest that contributes to Aias’s death.

l: Nemean Ode VIII, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: honors Deinis [winner in the short foot-race] Nemean Ode VIII celebrates Deinis of Aigina, winner of the short foot-race, and honors his father Meges. It invokes Aiakos and praises the enduring value of virtue, friendship, and song.

l: Deinis, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Deinis wins the short foot-race and receives a Lydian crown of song, celebrating races run with his father Meges.

l: Meges, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Meges, father of Deinis, receives a Lydian crown for two races and is honored with Deinis as song raises a lofty column for his house and Chariadai.

l: song, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Song raises a lofty column of praise for honored clans and warriors, making labor painless and preserving glory across time. Through lute, pipe, and poets’ work, it celebrates worthy deeds and victory, giving the dead an honorable name among children and townsfolk as a new winged hymn.

l: Nemean Ode IX, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: An ode celebrating Chromios of Aitna's chariot-race victory at Sikyon's local Pythian games, conventionally placed among the Nemeans despite its different setting.

l: the Pythian games at Sikyon, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: are_a local games The Pythian games at Sikyon are the local games in which Chromios won his chariot-race. The contest is identified as the event celebrated by the ode.

l: Chromios's chariot-race victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Chromios's chariot-race victory at Sikyon, crown of horse contests, wins prizes and crowns, inspiring a triumphal song, banquet, and celebration.

l: the triumphal procession to Aitna, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: originates_at Sikyon [from Apollo at Sikyon] The triumphal procession to Aitna carries the celebration from Apollo at Sikyon to the new city. It is directed toward Chromios's house, whose doors are opened to welcome visiting guests.

l: the victory song, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: A triumph song honors Chromios's chariot-race victory, performed with lyre and flute; it publicly records his good deed and renews the victory at a wine-filled banquet through praise and Charites' favor.

l: Theaios, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Theaios, son of Oulias, is a wrestler and victor at Argos. He first won at Pytho, then gained crowns at Isthmos and Nemea and twice at Athens; twice winning Hekatombaia at Argos brought relief from his labors.

l: Hekatombaia at Argos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_held_at Argos [festival] The Hekatombaia at Argos was the festival at which Theaios won his wrestling victory. Its contests included a struggle for the bronze shield and sacrifices of oxen to Hera.

l: wrestling-match, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_won_by Theaios The wrestling-match was won twice by Theaios, son of Oulias, at the Hekatombaia.

l: Lynkeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Lynkeus, Aphareus's son with the keenest eyes among men, watched Kastor and Polydeukes from Taygetos, fought Polydeukes by his father's sepulchre, and died from his bronze spear.

l: Idas, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_son_of Aphareus Idas, angered over oxen, struck Kastor with a bronze spear. He later faced Polydeukes beside his father's sepulchre and was killed by a thunderbolt from Zeus.

l: Argive athletic victories, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Argos is celebrated for numerous athletic victories, including those of Theaios at Pytho, the Isthmos, Nemea, the Gates of the Sea, the plains of Adrastos, and the festival of the Athenians. The city's champions also won prizes at Corinth, among the men of Kleonai, at Sikyon, Pellene, Kleitor, Tegea, among the Achaians' cities, and at Lykaion.

l: death of Kastor, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_caused_by Idas [Idas struck him with a bronze spearhead] Kastor was killed when Idas, angered over oxen, struck him with a bronze spear after Lynkeus saw the brothers in a hollow oak. Polydeukes found him not quite dead and appealed to Zeus for permission to share his brother's fate.

l: choice of Polydeukes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_to_share shared immortality of Kastor and Polydeukes [chosen in loyalty to Kastor] Polydeukes rejected the exclusive possibility of living in Olympos without death or old age. He chose instead to share equal time with Kastor, being alive beneath the earth for half the time and in the golden house of heaven for the other half.

l: shared immortality of Kastor and Polydeukes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: consists_of alternation between underworld and heaven [each brother spends half his time there] Kastor and Polydeukes received a shared existence through Polydeukes' choice. They dwell on alternate days with Zeus and in the hidden places beneath the earth at Therapnai, fulfilling an equal fate.

l: Aristagoras of Tenedos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Aristagoras of Tenedos, son of Arkesilas and member of a famous clan, is newly elected Prytanis and presides over the Senate of Tenedos. Welcomed to Hestia's sanctuary, he is prayed to finish his twelve-month term with fair fame and an unvexed heart. Praised for a splendid body, inherited dauntless heart, and sixteen wrestling and pankration victories, he missed the Pythian and Olympic Games through parental caution despite expected honor.

l: Tenedos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Tenedos, a city, is sustained by Aristagoras and fellow senators honoring Hestia and Zeus through sacrifices, music, songs, and rites.

l: Prytanis, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a President of the Senate [apparently] The Prytanis is presented as a kind of President of the Senate. Aristagoras assumes this office for a twelve-month term.

l: Senate of Tenedos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_led_by Prytanis [the Prytanis is its president] The Senate is represented by Aristagoras and his fellows, who draw near to Hestia's glorious sceptre during the initiatory ceremonies and honor her through sacrifices, music, songs, and ritual feasts.

l: election of the Prytanis, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: includes initiatory ceremonies [called [Greek: eisitaeria]] The election of the Prytanis occasions the ode for Aristagoras of Tenedos. His election is followed by initiatory ceremonies at which he is welcomed to Hestia's sanctuary.

l: initiatory ceremonies, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: mark election of the Prytanis [at the accession of a new Prytanis] The initiatory ceremonies accompany the election of a new Prytanis of Tenedos. During them, Aristagoras and his fellow senators approach Hestia's sanctuary and honor her with offerings, sacrifices, music, songs, and celebrations of Zeus's rites.

l: Hestia, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Hestia, daughter of Rhea and sister of highest Zeus, shares Hera’s throne and guards city halls, where senators are welcomed and she is honored through offerings, sacrifices, music, songs, and feasts.

l: sixteen neighboring athletic victories, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Sixteen illustrious victories among neighboring peoples have crowned Aristagoras and his famous clan in wrestling and in the pankration. These victories are presented as evidence of his strength and athletic distinction.

l: The Isthmian Odes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The Isthmian Odes are identified as the subject of this unit. No additional information about them is provided.

l: Herodotos of Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Herodotos of Thebes, son of Asopodoros and linked with Orchomenos, wins a chariot race by driving his four-horsed car unaided; honored for this victory, he seeks further athletic wreaths, fame, and honor for Thebes.

l: chariot race, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_won_by Herodotos of Thebes The chariot race is the contest in which Herodotos wins, driving his four-horsed car himself. Pindar presents the victory as worthy of praise and links it with the celebrated chariot skill of Kastor and Iolaos.

l: Herodotos' four-horsed car, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Herodotos’ four-horsed car wins victory, is honored by Pindar, and is driven unaided by Herodotos; Poseidon grants its speed.

l: Asopodoros, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Asopodoros, Herodotos’ father, seemingly banished from Thebes, is shipwrecked before Orchomenos, driven ashore, then rises again to better fortune.

l: Mortal excellence, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Mortal excellence, pursued with wealth and toil, earns praise and public recognition when achieved; it comes from Zeus, shifts with fortune and craft, yet noble deeds can preserve reputation beyond mortal life.

l: Thrasyboulos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Thrasyboulos, son of Xenokrates of Akragas, is the ode’s praised recipient, associated with hospitality and urged to speak of his father’s prowess as Nikesippos delivers the message.

l: chariot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_won_by Xenokrates of Akragas [at the Isthmian Games] Xenokrates won the chariot-race at the Isthmian Games. His chariot and the driving of the horses are praised, including the skill of Nikomachos, who managed the reins at Athens.

l: Isthmian Ode III, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: A victory song honoring Melissos of Thebes for pankration and chariot-race victories, praising his clan, invoking Herakles, and renewing ancient glory.

l: Melissos of Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Melissos of Thebes is a pankration victor trained by Orseas. Though small in stature, he is praised for lion-like courage, fox-like cunning, strength, and wrestling skill. After an earlier boys’ victory, he wins crowns at the Isthmian games and a Nemean chariot-race victory.

l: Nemean chariot victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Melissos wins a chariot-race in the hollow vale of the deep-chested lion, identified in the ode with Nemea. This victory, together with his Isthmian crown, gives him two prizes and allows him to proclaim Thebes as his home.

l: Kleonymid clan, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The Kleonymid clan is a Theban clan, descended from Kleonymos and maternally related to the Labdakidai. Known from the beginning for chariot racing, it loses four members in one day of war, declines, then regains glory through Melissos's victories.

l: Herakles's wrestling match with Antaios, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_compared_to pankration [Melissos's contest against his opponents] Herakles's match with Antaios serves as a comparison for Melissos's contest. Both Herakles and Melissos are presented as men of small stature whose courage, strength, and skill overcome larger or formidable opponents.

l: chariot, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The chariot is central to the Kleonymid clan's inherited athletic reputation. Kleonymos and his descendants compete with the curved chariot in major Greek contests, spend wealth on horses, and win victories at Athens, Sikyon, and Nemea.

l: Isthmian Ode IV, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: An ode for Phylakidas of Aigina, celebrating his pankration victory and praising Pytheas, Aigina, Aiakos’ sons, and honor through games and heroic deeds.

l: Theia, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Theia, Euruphaessa and chruse, is a many-named goddess, mother of Sun, Moon, and Morning; through her people prize gold and honor.

l: games, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: grant glory [through victory and wreaths] Games bring longed-for glory to those whose strong hands or swift feet win wreaths. The ode presents victory in games as a source of honor and celebrates Phylakidas’s success in them.

l: song of triumph, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a song [dispensed by the Muses in celebration of victory] The poet presents the ode as a triumphal song for Phylakidas and his family. He finally offers Lampon the sacred water of Dirke, symbolically giving him song made by the daughters of Mnemosyne.

l: Strepsiades of Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Strepsiades of Thebes is a pankratiast who wins the pankration at Isthmos; renowned for strength, shape, and valour, he shares his crown with his uncle.

l: pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_won_by Strepsiades of Thebes [at Isthmos] The pankration is the contest in which Strepsiades wins a prize at Isthmos.

l: Strepsiades's uncle, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Strepsiades’s uncle, also named Strepsiades, is Diodotos’s warrior son. He fights at the front, is praised with Meleagros, Hektor, and Amphiaraos, and dies in battle when Ares gives him over to death; valor earns enduring renown.

l: Kleandros, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Kleandros is a pankration competitor and victor, son of Telesarchos. He wins the pankration at the Isthmian Games, shows strength at the Nemean Games, and is honored at the games of Alkathoos and Epidauros. His toils bring a triumph song and a tender myrtle wreath before Telesarchos's house.

l: Telesarchos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_father_of Kleandros Telesarchos is identified as Kleandros’ father. His shining portal is the place before which the young men are urged to sing in honor of Kleandros.

l: Persians, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: are_expelled Hellas [finally expelled] The Persians had been finally expelled before the ode was written. Their defeat ended the terror that had caused the poet’s disquietude.

l: expulsion of the Persians, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: ends terror [the terror hanging over Hellas] The expulsion of the Persians brought an end to the terror that had hung over Hellas. The poet says that this relief permits people to set pleasant things before them despite earlier pain.

l: Nikokles, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Nikokles, Kleandros’s paternal uncle and a boxer, wins Dorian parsley at the Isthmian games; the Muses’ chariot proclaims his glory.

l: oracle concerning Thetis' son, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The oracle foretells that Thetis’ son will surpass his father and wield a fearsome bolt if she marries Zeus or his brothers; Themis therefore directs her marriage to Peleus.

l: Fragments, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Fragments are mostly unassigned; the remainder is divided among ten classes of songs and odes.

l: distinct classes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Nearly two-thirds of the Fragments cannot be assigned to any distinct class. The remaining Fragments are divided among ten distinct classes.

l: Epinikia (Triumphal Odes), The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a Triumphal Odes Epinikia are Triumphal Odes, such as the odes remaining to us entire.

l: Hymnoi (Hymns), The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Hymnoi are choice hymns, songs sung by a choir to honour gods; they sound for bright-filleted Semele when spring flowers appear at Argive Nemea.

l: Paianes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Paianes are hymns like Hymnoi, addressed especially to Apollo and Artemis, seeking their intervention against pestilence.

l: Dithyramboi, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Dithyramboi are choral songs of more general compass that sometimes verge on drama.

l: Prosodia (Processional Songs), The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a Processional Songs Prosodia are Processional Songs.

l: Parthenia (Songs for a Choir of Maidens), The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a Songs for a Choir of Maidens Parthenia are songs for a choir of maidens.

l: Hyporchaemata (Songs with Accompaniment of Dance), The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a Songs with Accompaniment of Dance Hyporchaemata are songs with accompaniment of dance.

l: Enkomia, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a Odes [sung by a komos in praise of some person, but not necessarily on any special occasion] Enkomia are odes sung by a komos in praise of some person, but not necessarily on any special occasion.

l: Skolia (Songs to be sung at Banquets), The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a Songs to be sung at Banquets Skolia are songs to be sung at banquets.

l: the blessed gods, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The gods in Olympus are invited to descend, dance, honor Athens, receive crowns and offerings, and watch the singer.

l: Bromios, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Bromios, an ivy-crowned god of clamorous shout, is invoked as the singer comes to sing for him.

l: offspring of Zeus and Kadmeän mothers, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: An offspring of Zeus and Kadmeän mothers, introduced as the subject the singer has come to sing.

l: spring, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Spring is a fragrant season whose approach is recognized by sacred palm branch tokens and whose arrival precedes Athens' vernal Dionysia.

l: temple of Zeus at Nemea, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The temple contained a sacred palm. Its priest could foresee from tokens of the palm’s branch that spring was approaching.

l: sacred palm, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: grows_in temple of Zeus at Nemea The sacred palm grew in the temple of Zeus at Nemea. A branch of it was given to a winner at the Nemean games together with the winner’s crown.

l: vernal Dionysia, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_in Athens The vernal Dionysia at Athens was associated with the approach of spring.

l: procession-song (prosodion), The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Fragments present a procession-song in honour of Delos.

l: Leto's children, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: are_children_of Leto [bright-haired Leto's children] Leto's children are described as bright-haired and as the blessed brood upon whom Leto looked after giving birth.

l: Leto's childbirth, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: takes_place_on Delos As Leto's childbirth drew near, four pillars sprang upright from roots deep down in the earth and held up the rock. Leto was delivered on Delos.

l: four pillars, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Four pillars with adamantine bases rise from deep roots when Leto's childbirth draws near and support a rock on their capitals.

l: fragment of a song with accompaniment of dance, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: A fragment of a song with dance accompaniment, written for a Sun eclipse, presents a prayer about the eclipse and its possible consequences for Thebes.

l: eclipse of the Sun, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Dated probably to April 30, B.C. 463, the eclipse of the Sun causes the Sun to hide during daytime, making wisdom’s paths and human strength seem useless, and is treated as a sign of fortune, war, destruction, or disaster.

l: the blessed dead, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The blessed dead are a group in their city, where some enjoy horses, bodily feats, dice, and harp-playing; they dwell beneath the shining sun amid fair-flowering bliss, incense, meadows, fruits, pleasures, and fragrance.

l: the body, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_subject_to the power of death [the great power] It is subject to the great power of death.

l: a shadow of life, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: An entity from the gods remains alive after the body dies, sleeps while limbs stir, and often reveals approaching judgment in dreams.

l: dreams, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: reveal the judgment [often to sleepers] They disclose at times the judgment that is drawing near for sorrow or for joy.

l: atonement, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_made_for an ancient woe It is made for an ancient woe and is accepted by Persephone.

l: an ancient woe, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: It is the cause for which atonement is made and accepted by Persephone.

l: souls, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Souls accepted by Persephone's atonement return to sunlight in the ninth year, then give rise to noble kings and swift, strong, wise men.

l: noble kings, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: are_called holy heroes [among men through the after-time] They spring from the souls sent back to the light of the sun above.

l: men swift and strong and in wisdom very great, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: are_called holy heroes [among men through the after-time] They spring from the souls sent back by Persephone and are later called holy heroes among men.

l: holy heroes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: are_called_in the after-time [among men] The noble kings and men swift, strong, and very wise are called holy heroes among men in the after-time.

l: end, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a conclusion The end is stated explicitly, signaling the conclusion of the document.

s: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies has title The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes has nurse nurse
q: For lo! I see come forth, suffused with tears, Orestes’ nurse.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes sees the Furies (as his mother’s hell-hounds)
q: These are no dreams, void shapes of haunting ill, But clear to sight my mother’s hell-hounds come!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Pylades supports Apollo (by urging Orestes to obey Apollo’s command)
q: Where then would fall the hest Apollo gave At Delphi, where the solemn compact sworn? Choose thou the hate of all men, not of gods.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra is a mother (of Orestes)
q: Stay, child, and fear to strike. O son, this breast Pillowed thine head full oft, while, drowsed with sleep, Thy toothless mouth drew mother’s milk from me.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra is a wife (of Agamemnon)
q: But she who plotted this accursèd thing To slay her lord, by whom she bare beneath Her girdle once the burden of her babes,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra murders Agamemnon (by craft and entanglement)
q: We slew by craft and by like craft shall die. Swift, bring the axe that slew my lord of old;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra is married to Aegisthus (as spouse and champion)
q: Woe, woe! Aegisthus, spouse and champion, slain!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Aegisthus is a usurper (ruling Agamemnon’s palace with Clytemnestra)
q: There lies our country’s twofold tyranny, My father’s slayers, spoilers of my home.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Aegisthus murders Agamemnon (with Clytemnestra)
q: They swore to work mine ill-starred father’s death, They swore to die together; ’tis fulfilled.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is exiled from Argos (as a child of banishment)
q: Whether to bear his dust unto his home, Or lay him here, in death as erst in life Exiled for aye, a child of banishment

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Aegisthus is killed by the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (as an adulterer and Agamemnon’s slayer)
q: He died the death law bids adulterers die.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Agamemnon is a king ships (the army’s lord)
q: O holy earth and holy tomb Over the grave-pit heaped on high, Where low doth Agamemnon lie, The king of ships, the army’s lord!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Agamemnon is killed in the bath
q: And next the kingly chief’s despite, When he who led the Greeks to fight Was in the bath hewn down.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Kilissa is a nurse (of Orestes)
q: Orestes’ nurse. What ho, Kilissa—thou Beyond the doors?

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Kilissa cherishes Orestes (from infancy)
q: Orestes dear, The day and night-long travail of my soul! Whom from his mother’s womb, a new-born child, I clasped and cherished!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Chorus is a servant women (of the palace)
q: Sister-servants, when draws nigh Time for us aloud to cry _Orestes and his victory?_

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Chorus supports Orestes (as avenger and liberator)
q: Nay, but the deed is well; link not thy lips To speech ill-starred, nor vent ill-boding words— Who hast to Argos her full freedom given, Lopping two serpents’ heads with timely blow.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the gods is bound by this law (Thou shalt not serve the wrong)
q: For even o’er Powers divine this law is strong— _Thou shalt not serve the wrong_. To that which ruleth heaven beseems it that we bow.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo foretells guilt of murder done should pass from me (if I slew)
q: Apollo, who foretold that if I slew, The guilt of murder done should pass from me;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo is associated with Delphi (as its prophetic god)
q: Unto Earth’s midmost shrine, the holy ground Of Loxias

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is dead no more
q: Strophius of Phocis; then he said, “Good sir, Since in all case thou art to Argos bound, Forget not this my message, heed it well, Tell to his own, _Orestes is no more_.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Argos is freed by the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (from the two usurpers)
q: Who hast to Argos her full freedom given, Lopping two serpents’ heads with timely blow.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: freedom restored to Argos is a political restoration (following the deaths of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus)
q: Hail to the commonwealth restored! Hail to the freedom won to me!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the curse of the house of Atreus is a hereditary doom (manifesting through successive murders)
q: And now the offspring of the race Stands in the third, the saviour’s place, To save—or to consume? O whither, ere it be fulfilled, Ere its fierce blast be hushed and stilled, Shall blow the wind of doom?

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies pursue Orestes (as avengers of his matricide)
q: But clear to sight my mother’s hell-hounds come!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is aided by Pylades (as his companion and counselor)
q: Can I my mother spare? speak, Pylades, PYLADES Where then would fall the hest Apollo gave At Delphi, where the solemn compact sworn?

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is commanded by Apollo (to avenge Agamemnon by killing Clytemnestra)
q: I say that rightfully I slew my mother, A thing God-scorned, that foully slew my sire And chiefest wizard of the spell that bound me Unto this deed I name the Pythian seer Apollo, who foretold that if I slew, The guilt of murder done should pass from me;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes commits the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (as vengeance for Agamemnon)
q: There lies our country’s twofold tyranny, My father’s slayers, spoilers of my home.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes possesses the sword (after killing Clytemnestra and Aegisthus)
q: The scene opens, disclosing Orestes standing over the corpses of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra; in one hand he holds his sword, in the other the robe in which Agamemnon was entangled and slain

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes possesses Agamemnon’s robe (the robe used to entangle Agamemnon)
q: The scene opens, disclosing Orestes standing over the corpses of Aegisthus and Clytemnestra; in one hand he holds his sword, in the other the robe in which Agamemnon was entangled and slain

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes experiences Orestes’ madness and vision of the Furies (after the murders)
q: Hark ye and learn—for what the end shall be For me I know not: breaking from the curb My spirit whirls me off, a conquered prey, Borne as a charioteer by steeds distraught Far from the course, and madness in my breast Burneth to chant its song, and leap, and rave

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo is a child of Zeus (as his son)
q: Gives voice to that which Zeus his sire decrees.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo possesses the oracle of Apollo (as its prophetic lord)
q: Unto the mighty Loxias, the lord Of this our shrine: healer and prophet he,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo protects Orestes (as his suppliant and guard)
q: Lo, I desert thee never: to the end, Hard at thy side as now, or sundered far, I am thy guard, and to thine enemies Implacably oppose me:

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo commands Orestes (to flee to Athens)
q: But unto Pallas’ city go, and there Crouch at her shrine, and in thine arms enfold Her ancient image:

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo orders the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (through his oracle)
q: Thine oracle bade this man slay his mother.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is a the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (a slayer of his mother)
q: For by my hest thou didst thy mother slay.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is pursued by the Furies (for matricide)
q: For they shall hunt thee through the mainland wide Where’er throughout the tract of travelled earth Thy foot may roam, and o’er and o’er the seas And island homes of men.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is brought before judges (for this cause)
q: there we well shall find Meet judges for this cause and suasive pleas, Skilled to contrive for thee deliverance From all this woe

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra is a ghost (of the slain mother)
q: the wandering ghost That once was Clytemnestra calls—Arise!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra seeks vengeance (for her killing)
q: Me doth no god arouse him to avenge, Hewn down in blood by matricidal hands.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: The Pythian Priestess uses the sacred chair (when consulting the oracle)
q: Then as a seeress to the sacred chair I pass and sit;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra is killed by Orestes (as his mother)
q: Orestes flies, who me, his mother, slew.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is a chorus (of avenging powers)
q: CHORUS OF FURIES

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is a ancient powers (older than the younger gods)
q: on the younger gods who tread down right, Sitting on thrones of might

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies dwells in Tartarus (as their dark abyss)
q: Yea, evil were they born, for evil’s doom, Evil the dark abyss of Tartarus Wherein they dwell,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is an avenger of the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (by pursuing the killer)
q: From home to home we chase the matricide.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies seeks vengeance (for the blood of Clytemnestra)
q: drawn on by scent of mother’s blood, Seek vengeance on this man and hound him down

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies pursues Orestes (from home to home)
q: From home to home we chase the matricide.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is excluded from these halls (where such as you can prowl)
q: These be no halls where such as you can prowl— Go where men lay on men the doom of blood,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena is wardress of the fane
q: On Pallas, wardress of the fane,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athens contains the Acropolis (site of Athena’s temple)
q: _The Scene of the Drama is the Temple of Apollo, at Delphi: afterwards the Temple of Athena, on the Acropolis of Athens, and the adjoining Areopagus._

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Justice requires wrath against them (for having their consort slain)
q: Therefore, if thou art placable to those Who have their consort slain, nor will’st to turn On them the eye of wrath, unjust art thou

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the marriage bond is guarded by Justice (as a sworn troth)
q: above the marriage-bed ordained For man and woman standeth Right as guard, Enhancing sanctity of troth-plight sworn;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the blood of Clytemnestra is sought by the Furies (as the basis of vengeance)
q: drawn on by scent of mother’s blood, Seek vengeance on this man and hound him down

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the trial of Orestes takes place in Athens (before appointed judges)
q: But unto Pallas’ city go, and there Crouch at her shrine, and in thine arms enfold Her ancient image: there we well shall find Meet judges for this cause

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Pythian Temple at Delphi contains the central altar
q: Lo, at the central altar I descry One crouching as for refuge—yea, a man

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Pythian Temple at Delphi contains the sacred chair (for the priestess)
q: Then as a seeress to the sacred chair I pass and sit;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Delphi rules this their land
q: And all this folk, and Delphos, chieftain-king Of this their land, with honour gave him home;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo is a prophet (of Zeus’s decrees)
q: And in his breast Zeus set a prophet’s soul, And gave to him this throne, whereon he sits, Fourth prophet of the shrine, and, Loxias hight, Gives voice to that which Zeus his sire decrees.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo is a healer (cleanser of homes)
q: Unto the mighty Loxias, the lord Of this our shrine: healer and prophet he, Discerner he of portents, and the cleanser Of other homes—behold, his own to cleanse!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is a Argive
q: An Argive am I, and right well thou know’st My sire, that Agamemnon who arrayed The fleet and them that went therein to war

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena is a goddess
q: And she, as goddess, from afar can hear,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena is a child of Zeus
q: O child of Zeus, one word shall tell thee all.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena possesses Athena’s aegis (as a divine attribute)
q: Hummed on the wind, instead of wings, the fold Of this mine aegis, by my feet propelled,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is a children of Night (by origin)
q: We are the children of eternal Night, And Furies in the underworld are called.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is a minister of Justice (in matters of bloodshed)
q: Of Justice are we ministers, And whosoe’er of men may stand Lifting a pure unsullied hand, That man no doom of ours incurs,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies pursues blood guilt (as avengers)
q: But if, as yonder man, he hath Blood on the hands he strives to hide, We stand avengers at his side,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies enforces vengeance (for blood shed within a family)
q: On him who slays we sweep with chasing cry: Though he be triply strong, We wear and waste him; blood atones for blood, New pain for ancient wrong.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is bound to Fate (by an ancient ordinance)
q: Fate, all-pervading Fate, this service spun, commanding That I should bide therein:

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is a son of Agamemnon (by lineage)
q: My sire, that Agamemnon who arrayed The fleet and them that went therein to war

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is excluded from the council And converse of Heaven’s lord
q: They may not strive with us who stand apart, A race by Zeus abhorred, Blood-boltered, held unworthy of the council And converse of Heaven’s lord.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra is the wife of Agamemnon (as his killer)
q: That Agamemnon, when he homeward came, Was brought unto no honourable death, Slain by the dark-souled wife who brought me forth To him,—enwound and slain in wily nets,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra is killed by Orestes (in retaliation for killing Agamemnon)
q: And I, returning from an exiled youth, Slew her, my mother—lo, it stands avowed!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athens contains Temple of Athena (on the Acropolis)
q: The scene changes to Athens. In the foreground, the Temple of Athena on the Acropolis;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Temple of Athena is located in Athens (on the Acropolis)
q: The scene changes to Athens. In the foreground, the Temple of Athena on the Acropolis;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Temple of Athena contains the statue of Athena (at its centre)
q: her statue stands in the centre; Orestes is seen clinging to it.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the statue of Athena is a refuge for Orestes (as a sacred suppliant place)
q: And clinging to thine image, bide my doom.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Hades is a realm of death (the Silent Land)
q: Till to the Silent Land, The realm of death, he cometh;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: blood guilt is punished by the Furies (in life and after death)
q: The price of blood, his hands have shed, We wring from him; in life, in death, Hard at his side are we!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is a matricide (as the perpetrator)
q: And I, returning from an exiled youth, Slew her, my mother—lo, it stands avowed!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Justice is administered by the trial of Orestes (through sworn judges)
q: I choose unto me judges that shall be An ordinance for ever, set to rule The dues of blood-guilt, upon oath declared.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Fate governs the Furies (in their inherited task)
q: Fate, all-pervading Fate, this service spun, commanding That I should bide therein:

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: vengeance is enacted by the Furies (for blood against kin)
q: On him who slays we sweep with chasing cry: Though he be triply strong, We wear and waste him; blood atones for blood, New pain for ancient wrong.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is pursued by the Furies (for killing his mother)
q: We chase from home the murderers of men.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is compelled by Loxias (to make the guilty meet their doom)
q: And in this deed doth Loxias bear part, Decreeing agonies, to goad my will, Unless by me the guilty found their doom.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is purified by the cleansing rite (after the matricide)
q: Long since have I this expiation done,— In many a home, slain beasts and running streams Have cleansed me.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is a suppliant of Athena (at her shrine)
q: And come at last, O Goddess, to thy fane, And clinging to thine image, bide my doom.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is a suppliant of the statue of Athena (seeking refuge)
q: Clasping this statue, as Ixion sat, A sacred suppliant for Zeus to cleanse,

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo cleanses Orestes (of blood-guilt)
q: Guest of my holy hearth and cleansed by me Of blood-guilt

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo commands the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (through his oracle, by Zeus’s authority)
q: The prophet-god bade thee thy mother slay? ORESTES Yea, and thro’ him less ill I fared, till now.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is a matricide (because he killed his mother)
q: I slew her. I deny no word hereof.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is son of Agamemnon
q: Slaying her husband, she did slay my sire.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes kills Clytemnestra (with a sword, by Apollo’s oracle)
q: Drawn sword in hand, I gashed her neck. ’Tis told.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is suppliant of Apollo (by sacred right)
q: First, as a witness come I, for this man Is suppliant of mine by sacred right

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is free from the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (by the court’s evenly divided vote)
q: Behold, this man is free from guilt of blood, For half the votes condemn him, half set free!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes is argive Argos (restored to his fatherland)
q: The man is Argive once again, and dwells Again within his father’s wealthy hall, By Pallas saved, by Loxias, and by Him, The great third saviour, Zeus omnipotent

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Orestes swears an oath to Athens (never to lead Argive forces against it)
q: Nevermore, Thro’ all the manifold years of Time to be, Shall any chieftain of mine Argive land Bear hitherward his spears for fight arrayed.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena is daughter of Zeus (born without a mother’s womb)
q: Birth may from fathers, without mothers, be: See at your side a witness of the same, Athena, daughter of Olympian Zeus, Never within the darkness of the womb Fostered nor fashioned, but a bud more bright Than any goddess in her breast might bear.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is a company of hell (grievous and ancient)
q: I rede ye well, beware! nor put to shame, In aught, this grievous company of hell.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies claims Justice (as its ancient right)
q: Since this young god o’errides mine ancient right, I tarry but to claim your law, not knowing If wrath of mine shall blast your state or spare

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies opposes Orestes (seeking his conviction for matricide)
q: Presumptuous is thy claim, blood-guilt to judge, And false henceforth thine oracles shall be.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the twelve judges decide the trial of Orestes (by casting votes)
q: Ye who judge, Arise, take each his vote, mete out the right, Your oath revering.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the council-court of judges is a tribunal (sacred and sworn)
q: Here to all time for Aegeus’ Attic host Shall stand this council-court of judges sworn, Here the tribunal, set on Ares’ Hill

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the council-court of judges is guardian of Athens (wakeful and protective)
q: Thus I ordain it now, a council-court Pure and unsullied by the lust of gain, Sacred and swift to vengeance, wakeful ever To champion men who sleep, the country’s guard.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Zeus is a Father of Olympian gods
q: Save what the Father of Olympian gods Commanded unto me.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Zeus commands Apollo (through Apollo’s prophetic office)
q: For never spake I from my prophet-seat One word, of man, of woman, or of state, Save what the Father of Olympian gods Commanded unto me.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena is champion of Orestes (as a man and father’s child)
q: For me no mother bore within her womb, And, save for wedlock evermore eschewed, I vouch myself the champion of the man, Not of the woman, yea, with all my soul,— In heart, as birth, a father’s child alone.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Zeus is father of Athena (without her being borne in a womb)
q: Athena, daughter of Olympian Zeus, Never within the darkness of the womb Fostered nor fashioned

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra kills Agamemnon (by guile with a covering net)
q: She spread from head to foot a covering net, And in the endless mesh of cunning robes Enwound and trapped her lord, and smote him down.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Clytemnestra is killed by Orestes (after killing his father)
q: Slaying her husband, she did slay my sire.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Agamemnon is killed by Clytemnestra (by female hands and a covering net)
q: She spread from head to foot a covering net, And in the endless mesh of cunning robes Enwound and trapped her lord, and smote him down.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus is justified by the prophet-god (bade thee thy mother slay)
q: The prophet-god bade thee thy mother slay? ORESTES Yea, and thro’ him less ill I fared, till now.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the killing of Orestes's father is caused by Slaying her husband
q: Slaying her husband, she did slay my sire.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the vote of the judges is equal to half the votes condemn him, half set free
q: For half the votes condemn him, half set free!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Justice is administered by the council-court of judges (through sworn judgment)
q: O men of Athens, ye who first do judge The law of bloodshed, hear me now ordain.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the oracle of Apollo commands the planned murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus (as a divine command)
q: The prophet-god bade thee thy mother slay?

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: fear and reverence protect Athens (by restraining injustice)
q: And hence shall Reverence and her kinsman Fear Pass to each free man’s heart, by day and night Enjoining, _Thou shalt do no unjust thing_, So long as law stands as it stood of old

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena establishes the council-court of judges (for all time in Athens)
q: Here to all time for Aegeus’ Attic host Shall stand this council-court of judges sworn, Here the tribunal, set on Ares’ Hill

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: lawful government requires fear and reverence (to prevent both lawlessness and tyranny)
q: Let no man live Uncurbed by law nor curbed by tyranny;_ Nor banish ye the monarchy of Awe Beyond the walls; untouched by fear divine, No man doth justice in the world of men.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Argos is bound by the oath between Argos and Athens (through Orestes’s pledge)
q: Nevermore, Thro’ all the manifold years of Time to be, Shall any chieftain of mine Argive land Bear hitherward his spears for fight arrayed.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena casts the vote of the judges (as the deciding vote for Orestes)
q: Mine is the right to add the final vote, And I award it to Orestes’ cause.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena declares Orestes (free from blood-guilt when the votes are equal)
q: Behold, this man is free from guilt of blood, For half the votes condemn him, half set free!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo is a prophet-god
q: For never spake I from my prophet-seat One word, of man, of woman, or of state, Save what the Father of Olympian gods Commanded unto me.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo is son of Zeus (subject to Zeus’s commands)
q: For never spake I from my prophet-seat One word, of man, of woman, or of state, Save what the Father of Olympian gods Commanded unto me.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Apollo supports Orestes (as witness, advocate, and protector)
q: First, as a witness come I, for this man Is suppliant of mine by sacred right, Guest of my holy hearth and cleansed by me Of blood-guilt: then, to set me at his side And in his cause bear part, as part I bore Erst in his deed, whereby his mother fell.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is deeply revered in courts of heaven and realms of hell
q: For mighty is the Furies’ power, And deep-revered in courts of heaven And realms of hell

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies protects Athens (as honored guardians of the city)
q: And ye and I will strive nor fail, That good may stand in evil’s stead, And lasting bliss for bale.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena is championed by Zeus (among the goddesses)
q: I too have Zeus for champion—’tis enough—

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena has access to Zeus (to the chamber storing his thunderbolts)
q: I only of all goddesses do know. To ope the chamber where his thunderbolts Lie stored and sealed

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena offers the Furies' sanctuary (as a permanent refuge in Athens)
q: For I, the queen of Athens’ sacred right, Do pledge to you a holy sanctuary Deep in the heart of this my land

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena establishes Athena's covenant with the Furies (through persuasion and pledges of honor)
q: And ye and I will strive nor fail, That good may stand in evil’s stead, And lasting bliss for bale.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena's covenant with the Furies offers mercy, gratitude and grace (within this land)
q: Such the boon I proffer thee—within this land of lands, Most loved of gods, with me to show and share Fair mercy, gratitude and grace as fair.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is a children of Night (by descent)
q: Ye too, O Fates, children of mother Night, Whose children too are we, O goddesses

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athens wins friends (in the land’s heart)
q: Then in the land’s heart shalt thou win thee friends.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athens receives Victory (as a divine gift)
q: But waft on us the gift and gain Of Victory divine!

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athens is free from civic strife (under the new settlement)
q: And nevermore these walls within Shall echo fierce sedition’s din Unslaked with blood and crime;

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Athena's citizens receives Justice (as the basis of civic security)
q: And ye shall make your town and land Sure, propped on Justice’ saving hand, And Fame’s eternity.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Zeus supports Athena (as her champion)
q: I too have Zeus for champion—’tis enough—

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the Furies is older than Athena (in age and ancient wisdom)
q: Older art thou than I, and I will bear With this thy fury. Know, although thou be More wise in ancient wisdom

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Justice protects Athens (as the foundation of civic stability)
q: And ye shall make your town and land Sure, propped on Justice’ saving hand, And Fame’s eternity.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the trial of Orestes is resolved by balanced vote
q: With balanced vote the cause had issue fair, Nor in the end did aught dishonour thee.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the trial of Orestes establishes Orestes' atonement (for the killing of Clytemnestra)
q: _Orestes slew: his slaying is atoned_.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the younger gods overrides the ancient gods (in the judgment concerning Orestes)
q: Woe on you, younger gods! the ancient right Ye have o’erridden, rent it from my hands.

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: the gods determines mortals (through fate and divine decrees)
q: For theirs it is by right to sway The lot that rules our mortal day

l: The House of Atreus; Being the Agamemnon, the Libation-Bearers, and the Furies
s: Earth supports Athens (as its fertile land)
q: For high shall be thine honour, set beside me For ever in this land, whose fertile lap Shall pour its teeming firstfruits unto you
